newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan recovery on track despite weak GDP data.
newsitem.headline: Japan recovery on track despite weak GDP data.

text.p: Japan's economy shrivelled in the three months to June after strong growth in the previous quarter, but the government said on Friday the data did not alter its view that the economy was still gradually recovering.

The government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- fell a real 0.7 percent in the April-June period from the previous quarter. This would translate into a drop of 2.9 percent on an annualised basis.
GDP measures the country's output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production.

"We have confirmed that there is steady private-sector capital spending, although consumption still lacks momentum. We are still moving in the direction of a gradual recovery," EPA Vice Minister Shinpei Nukaya said after the GDP announcement.

"We don't need to consider additional government spending for the economy following the latest GDP data for April-June," he added, challenging demands from some politicians eager to woo voters with an extra budget to stimulate the economy, ahead of imminent general elections.
Finance Minister Wataru Kubo told reporters on Friday morning that the government would decide next week if new steps were needed to keep the economic recovery on track.
First-half data showed annualised growth of 6.4 percent. In the January-March period, real GDP grew 2.9 percent quarter-on-quarter or an annualised 12.2 percent.
Looking at the components, housing investment showed steady growth on the back of low interest rates and a rush in demand ahead of a consumption tax rise next April.

Improvement in the growth of capital spending was also an encouraging sign that the economy was heading towards self-sustainable recovery, although private consumption fell compared to the previous quarter, which showed surprising growth due to the leap year effect.
"These numbers are within expectations, so there will be no change in the response of the markets," said Mikihiro Matsuoka, senior economist at Daiwa Institute of Research.

Economists agreed that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) would maintain its accommodative credit stance this year and perhaps into next year as well with these figures, a message the markets were waiting to confirm.

The dollar dipped against the yen in late Friday Tokyo dealings immediately after the release of the GDP data, but regained support on views that the data alone was not strong enough to alter the BOJ's monetary policy. Japanese government bonds were being bought in London trading.

Although Japan's inflation, measured by the GDP deflator, showed the first year-on-year increase in two years in the April-June quarter, a mere 0.3 percent rise "is not a risk in the Japanese economy," said Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan.
The government declared in February that the economy was gradually recovering after four years of negligible growth, but recent data has shown the recovery not gaining momentum.
"It's hard to think of any factors which would encourage a big rebound in the economic recovery (in the coming months)," said Hiroshi Suzuki, an economist at Norinchukin Research Institute.
"But it is not as if the recovery would falter. The basis is solid but the recovery is not spectacular. I think this condition would continue for the next year or so," he said.
The EPA's Nukaya remained confident that Japan would still be able to achieve its official target of 2.5 percent growth in the current fiscal year ending next March 31.
